root_cause.text: In mm/mempolicy's weighted_interleave_auto_store(), the existing wi_state was only retrieved in the !input branch, so the function's mode-match early return and old-state replacement logic operated without a valid old_wi_state, causing both the newly allocated new_wi_state and the replaced wi_state to be left unfreed.
root_cause.evidence: The patch moves `old_wi_state = rcu_dereference_protected(wi_state, ...)` outside the `if (!input)` block, adds `kfree(new_wi_state)` before the early return when `input == old_wi_state->mode_auto`, and the commit message explicitly states that with `"false"` the function returned early without freeing `new_wi_state`, while with `"true"` `old_wi_state` stayed NULL so `rcu_assign_pointer()` overwrote the old state and it was never freed.

intent_record.intent_summary: Fix weighted_interleave_auto_store() to free the newly allocated state on no-op updates and safely reuse the existing interleave table when present.
intent_record.what: The code moves the retrieval of old_wi_state via rcu_dereference_protected() out of the conditional block and performs it unconditionally after taking wi_state_lock. It adds an early-return check for the case where old_wi_state exists and input matches old_wi_state->mode_auto, and in that return path it now frees new_wi_state before returning. It also simplifies the !input branch so that copying old_wi_state->iw_table into new_wi_state->iw_table happens only when old_wi_state is non-NULL, then jumps to update_wi_state.
intent_record.how: At runtime, the function now avoids leaking the newly allocated new_wi_state when no mode change is needed and the function returns early. It also preserves previous iw_table contents when disabling auto mode if an old state exists, while still handling the no-old-state case safely.

This mode-match early return depends on old_wi_state being valid, but because old_wi_state was only fetched under !input, this check is part of the buggy path where the newly allocated state is returned without being freed on a no-op update.
This early return leaks the already allocated new_wi_state when the update is a no-op, since no cleanup occurs before returning.
This fetch of the existing wi_state is incorrectly placed inside the !input branch; the bug stems from not obtaining old_wi_state unconditionally before mode-match and replacement logic.

Author: Joshua Hahn <joshua.hahnjy@gmail.com>

    mm/mempolicy: Weighted Interleave Auto-tuning
    
    On machines with multiple memory nodes, interleaving page allocations
    across nodes allows for better utilization of each node's bandwidth.
    Previous work by Gregory Price [1] introduced weighted interleave, which
    allowed for pages to be allocated across nodes according to user-set

bic_trace_step.reason:
The function `weighted_interleave_auto_store()` clearly shows the vulnerable logic. It allocates `new_wi_state` up front (`new_wi_state = kzalloc(...)`) and initializes it, then takes `wi_state_lock`. However, `old_wi_state` is only assigned inside the `if (!input)` branch: `old_wi_state = rcu_dereference_protected(wi_state, lockdep_is_held(&wi_state_lock));`. In the `input == true` path, the code never retrieves the existing `wi_state` before executing `update_wi_state:` where it does `rcu_assign_pointer(wi_state, new_wi_state);`. Because `old_wi_state` remains NULL on that path, the old state that was replaced is never freed by the later cleanup block `if (old_wi_state) { synchronize_rcu(); kfree(old_wi_state); }`, causing a leak of the replaced state.

The early-return bug is also visible in the `!input` branch: after loading `old_wi_state`, the code checks `if (input == old_wi_state->mode_auto) { mutex_unlock(&wi_state_lock); return count; }`. Since this return happens after `new_wi_state` was allocated, but before it is freed, `new_wi_state` leaks on this mode-match early return. There is no `kfree(new_wi_state)` before returning.

So the function contains both aspects described in the root cause: retrieval of `old_wi_state` is limited to `!input`, and both the early return and replacement logic can leave allocations unfreed. Therefore the vulnerable construct is present, and the fix is not yet present.
